https://youtu.be/krBvYTfxJks?si=ju_-Cbkv.text: I have lipodema (only stage 1) and have greatly reduced swelling and problems through bike riding for exercise (1-1.5 hours several times a week, if not daily), and intermittent fasting 16 hours a day. I also stopped red meat and almost never eat chicken. I eat whole foods for the most part (occasional cheating on chips or a homemade cookie  or sweet roll seems to be OK as long as it's rare). Never eat processed food. I lost 15 pounds without "dieting", I just eat well, don't eat after 7pm and fast until 11am., then I eat as much as I want. I have olive oil in my diet, eat lots of vegetables, beans, nuts, and fruits. I make homemade granola with healthy fats and a small amount of honey or maple syrup (it doesn't taste sweet, and I've gotten used to it because I make it crunchy and toasty and eat with apples and berries). I eased into all of the above over several years, and I don't think anyone can jump in and change heaven and earth and have it work. Begin by increasing the good and decreasing the harmful. Feeling good and being healthy reinforces good eating. Don't judge yourself, just try to do better the next day!

As someone who was born with lipedema plus Morbus Hashimoto plus Neurodermitis, alongside a severe but late discovered gluten & soy intolerance, plus less severe but still noticeable casein and ovalbumin intolerance -- I eat Paleo which includes read meat and chicken to cover my proteins for the day (always been the fit person) without causing troubles for my lectins. Cycling where I live is not always possible due to climate reasons. 

The liposuctions were the relief I was looking for. Plain and simple.

All those tips to "just be better next time" to tweak and hack and optimize and somersault my diet and lifestyle into impossible standards of uber perfection were doing the opposite; they made me physically ill, and stressed out to a point of developing an eating disorder - because none of that shit worked for me at all. 

Now I'm lipo'd and without any crazy starving myself, no calorie counting (it's seriously so harmful and obsessive when you think about it) and walking up to women to see whether they might be as frustrated as I once was, and point out lipedema to them and that it actually isn't their fault after all if they can't lose fat. Chill paleo diet with the occasional processed soul food during my cycle (pms has gotten SO much better after the surgeries, too) + exercising my sports. 
Far from ideal, still a lifetime of hard work and maintenance but things are mostly under control and I've made peace with my diagnoses.

Pecan and Coconut Granola

16 cups regular rolled oats 
3 cups roughly chopped pecans
3 cups roughly chopped almonds
8 cups unsweetened coconut chips
3/4 cup hemp seeds (double if desired)
1.5 c ground flax seeds
2 heaping T cinnamon
1)Diamond kosher salt (more or less to taste)
1 cup sorghum (or maple syrup or c honey)
1 c avo or sunflower oil

Preheat oven to 275. 
Mix all the oats and nuts and salt in a large bowl. Pour half the syrup and oil over it and mix. Repeat. 

Spread out mixture on two large rimmed baking sheets covered with parchment and bake on two oven racks until golden. Stir, switch racks and repeat as needed. I cook the granola until it’s pretty dark and crunchy. Add in cherries or other dried fruit after cooking if desired, or add raisins when eating it. 

When cool, put in sealed containers and store on the shelf or in the freezer if you won't finish it soon.

You must elevate your legs everyday. You must talk to your doctor. You may have some heart & circulation issues going on. Make an appointment. 

Compression socks really need to be prescribed by a doctor. The improper compression CAN hurt you vs help you. 
There are mild compression  15-20  socks that you can use and they will help. BUT..  you may have underlying issues, including heart issues that are starting. It is important to find out now before they get worse. 

About your legs… are they hard to reduce in size? Have they always been larger?  Do your legs feel heavy as the day progresses? Heavy as in difficult to lift.  Is the skin on your ankles  turning a darker color? Do your legs hurt? Do you have what you think is cellulite on your upper legs? 

Are you overweight? Is your body pear shaped? Do you smoke? Drink alcohol? Eat fatty foods??

If you have lymphedema or similar conditions, the best doctor to see is a HEART specialist. They deal with these issues everyday.  Basic primary care doctors usually tell you to lose weight. Heart doctors have trained nurses that can apply proper compression on your legs to keep your swelling down. Your heart doctor may prescribe leg pumps to use once a day to help your legs from swelling. 

If you are diagnosed with lymphedema you must be treated with experienced therapists and doctors.  NEVER take water pills if you have Lymphedema.  Most regular doctors do not know this!!

MCAS is a common comorbidity for folks with EDS / Hypermobility...who also commonly get lipedema/lymphedema. On top of that, we often get POTS (which means we are encouraged to consume high amounts of salt to regulate our symptoms, so we cannot easily cut it from our diets). This advice seems great for folks with "just" lipedema /lymphedema, but it doesn't seem to fully account for the complicated co-morbidities we frequently get.

Beef tallow is not a rich source of polyunsaturated fatty acids, with only 3.45 percent in grain-fed and 1.9 percent of the total in grass-fed.

Thus, while even grain-fed beef tallow has a much lower content of polyunsaturated fatty acids than modern vegetable oils, the amount found in grass-fed tallow is much lower and similar to that found in the coconut products that dominate the traditional diets of Pacific Islanders, who have been extensively studied and shown to be free of heart disease. This would allow the use of tallow in the context of a mixed diet that includes other foods naturally rich in polyunsaturated fatty acids, such as fatty fish, while still keeping the overall intake of these fatty acids low and similar to that found in successful traditional diets.

Grass-fed beef is often promoted as healthy because of a lower saturated fatty acid content. But saturated stearic acid was 36 percent higher in grass-fed beef (17.45 percent versus 12.8 percent). Levels of sixteen-carbon palmitic acid, considered “atherogenic” because in some studies it raises cholesterol levels slightly, were virtually the same in both samples. Thus, in equally fatty cuts of beef, there would be a higher content of saturated fatty acids in the grass-fed beef. In many traditional diets where the fattiest cuts and the fat itself were sought out, intake of these saturates would likely be considerably higher.

Lymphedema and lipedema, while both involving swelling, have distinct characteristics and underlying mechanisms. Recent research suggests the skin and gut microbiome may play a role in the development and progression of these conditions. Altered microbial composition and increased inflammation related to the microbiome have been observed in both lymphedema and lipedema, potentially impacting lymphatic function and fat tissue distribution. 
Lymphedema is characterized by swelling due to lymphatic system dysfunction, often resulting from damage or blockage of lymphatic vessels. This can lead to fluid and protein buildup in the tissues, causing swelling, pain, and increased risk of infection. Secondary lymphedema can be acquired through cancer treatment, surgery, trauma, or infection, while primary lymphedema has a genetic component. 
Lipedema is a chronic condition primarily affecting women, characterized by symmetrical swelling of the limbs due to abnormal fat tissue accumulation and lymphatic system involvement. Lipedema is often misdiagnosed as obesity, but unlike obesity, it is characterized by disproportionate fat distribution, pain, and easy bruising. Lipedema can also lead to secondary lymphedema. 

The microbiome's role:
Skin Microbiome:
Studies have shown that the skin microbiome in individuals with lymphedema can exhibit altered bacterial composition and increased heterogeneity. In some cases, specific bacterial genera like Propionibacterium and Streptococcus show high variability between limbs affected by lymphedema and healthy limbs, suggesting a potential link between the skin microbiome and lymphatic dysfunction.
 
Gut Microbiome:
The gut microbiome, a complex ecosystem of bacteria, plays a crucial role in overall health and inflammation. Research suggests that the gut-lymphatic axis, the connection between the gut and the lymphatic system, is a key area of investigation. Bacterial-triggered immune activation can influence lymphatic function and potentially contribute to both lymphedema and lipedema. 

Inflammation:
Both lymphedema and lipedema are associated with inflammation. The gut and skin microbiome can influence inflammation levels, and imbalances in the microbiome may contribute to chronic inflammation in these conditions. 

Potential implications:
Targeted therapies:
Understanding the role of the microbiome in lymphedema and lipedema could lead to the development of targeted therapies that modulate the microbiome to reduce inflammation, improve lymphatic function, and manage fat tissue distribution.
 
Dietary interventions:
Dietary modifications, including prebiotics, probiotics, and synbiotics, may help modulate the gut microbiome and potentially impact the progression of lymphedema and lipedema, according to a study on synbiotics. 

Personalized medicine:
Further research into the microbiome in lymphedema and lipedema could pave the way for more personalized approaches to treatment, considering individual microbial profiles and responses to interventions. 

In summary, while lymphedema and lipedema are distinct conditions, emerging research suggests the microbiome plays a significant role in their development and progression. Further research into the interplay between the microbiome, inflammation, and lymphatic function may lead to new therapeutic strategies and personalized approaches to managing these conditions.

To effectively manage lymphedema and lipedema through diet, focus on an anti-inflammatory, whole-foods approach, prioritizing plant-based foods, minimizing processed items, and identifying and eliminating individual trigger foods, while consulting with healthcare professionals for personalized guidance. 
Key Dietary Strategies:

Prioritize Whole Foods:
Emphasize fresh, unprocessed foods, particularly a variety of fruits and vegetables, especially those with vibrant colors, as they are rich in nutrients and antioxidants. 
Minimize Added Sugars and Refined Carbohydrates:
Avoid or limit added sugars, especially fructose, and refined grains, such as white bread, pasta, and rice, as these can contribute to inflammation and weight gain. 

Limit Processed Foods:
Processed foods often contain unhealthy fats, excessive salt, and additives, which can exacerbate inflammation and fluid retention. 

Consider Fermented Foods:
Fermented foods like kefir and yogurt can be beneficial for gut health, which is closely linked to lymphatic function. 

Focus on Healthy Fats:
Include sources of healthy fats like omega-3s found in fish (salmon), nuts, and seeds, while limiting unhealthy fats like those found in fried foods and processed snacks. 

Stay Hydrated:
Drink plenty of water throughout the day to support lymphatic drainage and overall health.
 
Identify and Eliminate Trigger Foods:
Experiment with eliminating common inflammatory triggers like gluten, dairy (especially for lipedema), and caffeine to see if they improve symptoms. 

Intermittent Fasting:
Intermittent fasting, when appropriate and under professional guidance, may help with weight management and potentially reduce inflammation. 

Consult with Professionals:
Work with a registered dietitian or other healthcare professional specializing in lymphatic conditions to develop a personalized dietary plan that addresses your specific needs and health status. 

Avoid Fad Diets:
Fad diets are often unsustainable and can be detrimental to overall health. Focus on creating a healthy eating pattern that you can maintain long-term.

What is the difference between lipedema and lymphedema?
Lipedema vs Lymphedema: What's the Difference.
Lipedema and lymphedema are both conditions that can cause swelling in the limbs, but they are distinct conditions with different causes and characteristics. Lipedema is a chronic condition causing abnormal fat accumulation, mainly in the legs and sometimes arms, while lymphedema is a fluid retention issue due to lymphatic system damage. 

Lipedema:
Cause: Abnormal fat accumulation, primarily in the legs and sometimes arms, often in a disproportionate manner. 
Swelling: Non-pitting (no indentation when pressed) and symmetrical, often with a "cuff" of fat around the ankles. 

Other symptoms: Pain, tenderness, and easy bruising in the affected areas. 
Typically affects: Primarily women, and often not the feet. 

Progression: Can worsen over time and lead to mobility issues and joint pain. 
Stemmer's sign: Negative (skin can be pinched above the toe). 

Lymphedema:
Cause: Damage or blockage to the lymphatic system, leading to fluid buildup in the tissues. 

Swelling: Pitting edema (indentation when pressed), often asymmetrical and may affect the hands and feet. 
Other symptoms: Heaviness, tightness, skin changes (hardening, thickening), and increased risk of skin infections. 

Typically affects: Can occur in various parts of the body, but often in the limbs (arms or legs). 
Progression: Can worsen over time and lead to more severe swelling and tissue damage. 

What foods aggravate lipedema?
Factors Exacerbating Lipedema: Triggering Drugs, Foods, and ...
Foods That Worsen Lipedema

Foods high in salt can cause water retention, worsening lipedema complaints. Sugary and processed foods can trigger fat accumulation and increase inflammation, which may accelerate the progression of lipedema.

https://youtu.be/krBvYTfxJks?si=ju_-Cbkv.text: Frances  Hello, I went to Stanford exactly 20 years ago after developing bi-lateral lower extremity LE. NOW only in right leg and foot. They were awesome. Can’t say enough about them and their level of care and knowledge. Dr Rockson was my physician as well as Dr Szuba. Anyway, 2 weeks of intensive lymphatic decongestive therapy, learning to wrap properly, Reid sleeves for night sleeping, and custom compression stockings. The lymphoscintigraphy test was extremely painful for me bc they inject a dye between each of your toes and my right foot/toes are swollen. Hurt like hell. Left foot not so bad. You can look that test up. They want to track your lymphatic system so about every 20 minutes you go in the imaging machine so they can see where that fluid goes. It takes a long time to complete the testing. All I can say is that Stanford is worth going to. Highly recommend it and I haven’t forgotten a thing I learned. I have had to educate drs and even physical therapists since Stanford. Actually I TELL them what I need and they just do it. 😀 I am very forceful and know my body. Had horrible PT’s in the past, prior to and after Stanford. I haven’t been to PT or a Dr for LE since 2001 except for prescription for custom thigh high’s. Eating right is important. Intuitively I knew what not to eat even though many physical therapists told me there was “no studies” indicating sugar, White foods, processed foods, fried foods, etc were bad. I just stopped ingesting all that. Exercise is extremely important and I was told from 1998-2000 that exercise was not good for LE. I was a gym whore. I became very depressed. So all I can say is listen to your inner voice. And join LE&RN and watch these videos from Dr Rockson and other professionals. I was in law enforcement and exactly at age 38 when I developed LE. Thought I’d never make it to retirement. But through Stanford and listening to myself and educating myself, I made it. Have faith. Many of the videos I watch on YouTube from so-called professional or educated LE therapists have no clue how to wrap a leg. So beware of who you watch. Some are down right ignorant and dangerous. If you ever want to talk, let me know. I know what it’s like to not have any one to help you, dismiss you, or understand you. Good luck. You’ll love Stanford. Soak it in and bring a list of questions.
